📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Several decades after World War II ended, this harrowing historical occurrence has remained an key part of modern global discourse. Thanks to the media, we're constantly given a front-row seat to bits and pieces of the event that arguably had the most influence in shaping our world as we know it today. The year so far has delivered its fair share of acclaimed WWII projects, from Tom Hanks' World War II with Tom Hanks docu-series to Brendan Fraser's Pressure and, more recently, Netflix's The Mosquito Bowl, starring Bill Skarsgård. A couple more titles are still expected before the year winds down, but unfortunately, the most anticipated one is missing from that list.

Recent findings suggest that back in 2022, the BBC brought its audiences what would instantly be deemed one of the greatest WWII series since Steven Spielberg and Hanks' miniseries, Band of Brothers. Band of Brothers was a masterclass in TV-making that drew comparisons to another legendary work, Saving Private Ryan, thanks to its high production value and visceral depiction of wartime horrors. Several follow-up efforts to recapture its essence were released to mixed to average reception until the BBC premiered SAS: Rogue Heroes. Created by Steven Knight (Peaky Blinders), SAS: Rogue Heroes has earned universal acclaim, with a rare 100% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes for Seasons 1 and 2.

Season 3 had been in production for some time, and reports of an early 2026 wrap had fans wishing for a late 2026 return. However, it's now official that the acclaimed war series will follow its usual Upcoming Year's release window, with the BBC officially reporting that SAS: Rogue Heroes Season 3 will be released in 2027. Alongside the announcement came first-look stills at what to expect from Season 3. The new photos, which can be seen below, feature a host of returning characters including Paddy Mayne (Jack O’Connell), Reg Seekings (Theo Barklem-Biggs), Jim Almonds (Corin Silva), Pat Riley (Jacob Ifan), Bill Fraser (Stuart Campbell) and John Tonkin (Jack Barton).

It has been revealed that season 3 of the series, adapted from Ben Macintyre's best-selling non-fiction book, will pick up from the events of the Season 2 finale, which saw the gallant SAS heroes parachuting towards Nazi-occupied France. The fresh chapter opens in the summer of 1994 in France, where they have now landed deep behind enemy lines to destroy the German forces and repel Allied advances. The brave men will yet again confront insurmountable challenges in their mission to free Western Europe.

Sources indicate that they will team with the French resistance, as well as members of the Maquis, to be played by a fresh cast including Bérangère McNeese (Miles & Juliette) and Hélie-Rose Dalmay (The Intruder). Other newcomers arriving in Season 3 include the characters Reverend Fraser McLuskey (Lorne MacFadyen) and an American soldier named Silus Roe, to be played by Nick Hargrove (American Primeval); all of whom can be spotted in the gallery above.

SAS: Rogue Heroes Season 3 will premiere on the BBC and BBC iPlayer on a yet-to-be-declared 2027 date, likely in January, and will stream in the US on MGM+. Stay tuned for future updates.

GTA 6 Is So Unstoppable It's Even Made Nickelback Go Viral

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (590 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's still a debate whether Grand Theft Auto 6 has the best gaming soundtrack of 2026, but it certainly has the most soundtrack of 2026.
  • Thanks to GTA 6, Nickelback's 2001 angst ballad "How You Remind Me" has been getting a lot of play — kind of.
  • Recent findings suggest that you might be somewhat surprised to hear "How You Remind Me" making the rounds again, years removed from its days reigning over the Billboard charts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's still a debate whether Grand Theft Auto 6 has the best gaming soundtrack of 2026, but it certainly has the most soundtrack of 2026. Rockstar Games' latest open-world crime epic features more than 800 songs, most of which you'll hear on its 26 genre-themed radio stations. Of all this breadth of wild music, you'd figure the most popular song on the soundtrack would be something that had overlap with a Fast and Furious OST. But it turns out the single best song in the GTA 6 soundtrack is something by... Nickelback?

Thanks to GTA 6, Nickelback's 2001 angst ballad "How You Remind Me" has been getting a lot of play — kind of. Technically, this version is a cover. GTA 6's Kaleidoscope FM radio station plays alternate-language versions of popular songs, the indisputable best of which is "Ola Afta Poui Fovamai," by the Greek singer and alternate former tourism minister Alkistis Protopsalti. As far as covers go, this is one for the ages. Seriously, listen:.

Recent findings suggest that you might be somewhat surprised to hear "How You Remind Me" making the rounds again, years removed from its days reigning over the Billboard charts. To this day, the most-played radio song of the 2000s has been relegated to background music in the daddest bars from Mississauga to Massapequa. It is arguably the epitome not just of Dad Rock but specifically of Divorced Dad Rock. If "How You Remind Me" was a person, its kitchen would include Slim Jims (assorted flavors), cold pizza (definitely pepperoni), and nothing else. It would drive a 2014 Corvette Stingray (bright red, obviously). It would live on the golf course.

But with "Ola Afta Poui Fovamai," Protopsalti injects a youthful, upbeat verve to Chad Kroeger's genius composition that legendarily emerged, nearly fully formed, from his brain in just 45 minutes following an argument with a partner. It's the sort of track you'd play in a convertible on a sunny day, or in the bathroom while getting ready for a party themed after The Devil Wears Prada (the good one). There is practically zero Divorced Dad energy in "Ola Afta Poui Fovamai." It is transformational.

I am far from the only person to completely lose my shit over the resurfacing of a song that hit number-one on charts in Austria, Canada, Denmark, Ireland, and the United Kingdom, in addition to peaking in the top ten in various other international markets. As of this writing, searches for "Nickelback" on Bluesky are all about "Ola Afta Poui Fovamai." On Facebook, Greek culture accounts are sharing the cover as a point of national pride. When Canadian streamer Dan "Greenskull" Hammill heard it for the first time in-game, he burst into a karaoke rendition that has since gone semi-viral.

Truth told, the Canadian rock quartet legitimately is one of my guilty pleasures. As a teenager, I once suffered a pretty serious concussion in a skiing accident; according to the paramedics, I spent the entire ride to the hospital singing "Photograph" in my unconscious state. Mortifying, but also hard to deny. Such is the allure of GTA 6. In being a mirror of our world, it's also a mirror of our lives, thus revealing truths we may not have otherwise been ready to admit. The boyfriends of the world start doing more chores for their partners. Those of us who've let the gym routine fall by the wayside pick it back up again. Nickelback? A guilty pleasure? I no longer see anything to be guilty about here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, spider-Man has teamed with a lot of superheroes over the decades, so much so that this is literally the premise of the multiple Marvel Team-Up volumes. Yet, for a long time, Spidey shied away from officially joining a superhero team. That changed in the 2000s when Peter Parker joined the New Avengers, and since then he’s rotated in and out of the Earth’s Mightiest Heroes roster. Now he’s not only back on the team, but leading it.

Industry observers note that following the events of Avengers: Armageddon, a new incarnation of the Avengers has formed, though it's one that’s keeping a lower profile due to the public’s distrust towards superheroes. This time, Spidey is calling the shots, but his tenure as leader has already gotten off to a horrible start. That’s evident by how he’s facing resistance from the other Avengers in the next issue of The Amazing Spider-Man.

According to recent reports, at the end of The Amazing Spider-Man #1003, J. Jonah Jameson was kidnapped by Itsy Bitsy, a warped clone made up of Spider-Man and Deadpool’s genetic material. Despite Jameson having been one of the Web-Slinger’s closest allies ever since learning he was Peter Parker during Chip Zdarsky’s Spectacular Spider-Man run, the media figure has returned to badmouthing Spider-Man on air to boost ratings. Itsy Bitsy didn’t take kindly to this and kidnapped him, and in the preview for The Amazing Spider-Man #1004, she ignores Jameson’s pleas to free him.

In a recent development, spider-Man highlights Luke Cage, Daredevil, Wolverine, Captain Marvel, and Miracleman the livestream of Itsy Bitsy torturing Jameson and allowing viewers to bet on what will come of this gruesomeness. Unfortunately for Spidey, his fellow Avengers scoff at his call to band together and rescue Jameson, feeling it’s not worth their time. They’re busy with other things, including Miracleman breaking up a HYDRA cell, Luke dealing with Subterraneans in the Upper West Side, and Captain Marvel clashing with the Serpent Society.

Industry observers note that though he apologizes to everyone for calling them away from their other concerns (except for Daredevil, whom it’s implied was simply meeting up for one of his romantic rendezvouses with Elektra), Spider-Man reminds them he’s the Avengers’ leader, so this mission to rescue Jameson should take priority. Judging from the solicitation for The Amazing Spider-Man #1005, it seems like all but Wolverine will nonetheless leave him in the lurch. That doesn’t bode well for Spidey being taken seriously as a leader.

It has been revealed that even though this is Spider-Man’s first time leading the Avengers, he has experience being in charge of a group of people. Most notably, he’s been the anchoring hero of Marvel’s Spider-Verse events, led different incarnations of the Fantastic Four when the main quartet has been absent, and he even assembled The Outlaws, comprised of Sandman and Rocket Racer, at a time when he felt he couldn’t trust the Avengers. In his civilian life, Peter also took over running Parker Industries after Doctor Octopus’ consciousness left his body.

Sources indicate that what makes Spider-Man’s tenure as the Avengers’ leader challenging is that, as mentioned earlier, the world is leery towards superheroes after the previous Avengers’ fight with Red Hulk led to thousands dying in Europe. The United Nations passed a resolution banning superpowers, and while the United States abstained from signing this, that’s only because roughly 80% of enhanced individuals live within its borders. Even then, the UN-funded S.H.I.E.L.D. is restricting the Avengers and other superheroes from operating outside the States.

As a result, the Avengers have to be cautious about what missions they take on, and the majority are in agreement that rescuing Jameson from Itsy Bitsy is, as Florence Pugh’s Yelena Belova put it in Spider-Man: Brand New Day, “small potatoes.” If Luke Cage, Daredevil, Wolverine, Captain Marvel, and Miracleman are already pushing back against Spidey’s orders this early, it’s possible this is indicative of how he’ll be treated in the main Avengers title. If Spider-Man can’t be properly respected as the team’s leader, then this version of the Avengers won’t be able to function properly.

The Amazing Spider-Man #1004 will be released Wednesday, November 25 by Marvel Comics.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Steven Spielberg has directed musicals, sci-fi epics, adventure films, and biopics, but one genre has eluded him over the course of his decades-long career. He has never directed a Western, despite having openly longed to put his spin on the type of movies that turned one of his idols, John Ford, into a legend.

Industry observers note that well, the wait is over. Spielberg is developing an untitled film for Focus Features about two fugitives charting a course across the American West, and he’s assembled a crack team to help him. The ensemble will include Jessie Buckley, fresh off her Oscar win for “Hamnet,” Cillian Murphy, the Oscar-winning star of “Oppenheimer,” and Mark Rylance, a frequent Spielberg collaborator who won, you guessed it, an Oscar for “Bridge of Spies.” Related Stories ‘Focker In-Law’ Review: An Eager Ariana Grande Isn’t Enough to Save a Comedy Sequel That Can’t Remember What People Liked About This Franchise Jane Fonda on Documentary ‘Gaslit,’ Trump, and What the Democrats’ Midterm Victory Means for Climate Change.

It has been revealed that but there’s more to get cinephiles’ hearts racing! Paul Thomas Anderson, the Oscar-winning filmmaker behind “Boogie Nights,” “There Will Be Blood,” and “One Battle After Another,” is writing the script. It’s based on Kevin Barry’s novel, “The Heart in Winter.” Though Anderson usually directs his screenplays, he’s done script doctoring for Ridley Scott (“Napoleon”) and Martin Scorsese (“Killers of the Flower Moon” and the upcoming “What Happens at Night”). He also did some work on “Corky Romano” — hey, they can’t all be winners! So why not join Spielberg’s merry band?

It has been revealed that spielberg is still one of the all-time greats, but he could use a hit. “Disclosure Day,” which marked his return to summer movies, was a box office disappointment, and his most recent films, like “The Fabelmans” and “West Side Story,” struggled to connect with audiences despite earning excellent reviews. Maybe saddling up will be just what the movie gods ordered.

Kristie Macosko Krieger, Sara Murphy, Anderson, and Spielberg will produce the film, which is expected to hit theaters in 2028. Tim Headington, Neil Shah, Ryan Zacarias, and Ana Leocha will executive produce it.

But all of the specs it does have are enough to run the things you need on iPadOS. If someone on your list is looking for an iPad for web browsing, streaming, messaging, and light gaming—and they don't need something for professional work—this device is likely more than enough iPad for them.

Tom Hardy And Gary Oldman Had A Batman Reunion In This Forgotten Western Gangster Movie

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when you think of Tom Hardy and Gary Oldman working together, chances are you think of 2012's "The Dark Knight Rises," in which they played Bane and Commissioner James Gordon, respectively.
  • Industry observers note that today, Hardy and Oldman happen to be on two of the best reveals on TV.
  • Unfortunately, the pair don't actually share any scenes in the film, but their respective presences help elevate the whole affair, which is well worth a watch for the quietly intense performance from Hardy and the signature flourish of a performance from Oldman.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when you think of Tom Hardy and Gary Oldman working together, chances are you think of 2012's "The Dark Knight Rises," in which they played Bane and Commissioner James Gordon, respectively. But this generation-spanning British duo have crossed paths on screen multiple times throughout the years, including in a movie that debuted the same year as their Batman team-up. Yes, "The Dark Knight Rises" was one of two films in 2012 to give us a Hardy/Oldman collab (as well as a weird Tom Hardy accent). The other was "Lawless," a Southern Gothic gangster outing that's been mostly forgotten, but was a fairly big deal at the time.

Industry observers note that today, Hardy and Oldman happen to be on two of the best reveals on TV. The former plays the perpetually embattled mob fixer Harry Da Souza on "MobLand," and the latter plays the perpetually disheveled Jackson Lamb on "Slow Horses." But the duo have worked together on four separate projects throughout their careers, beginning with one of the greatest spy movies ever made: 2011's "Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy." Asked by Digital Spy about working with Oldman on the John le Carré adaptation, Hardy had nothing but praise for the man. "Gary Oldman is my hero, that's it," he remarked. "He's right up there." The actor went on to say he's "stolen everything" from Oldman, with whom he'd re-team a year later on "Lawless.".

Unfortunately, the pair don't actually share any scenes in the film, but their respective presences help elevate the whole affair, which is well worth a watch for the quietly intense performance from Hardy and the signature flourish of a performance from Oldman.

"Lawless" is directed by John Hillcoat, who made his breakthrough by overseeing one of the best dark Westerns ever made: "The Proposition." That 2005 effort was written by Nick Cave, who also penned the script for "Lawless," based on Matt Bondurant's historical novel "The Wettest County in the World." It's a lot less brutal than Hillcoat's 2005 effort, and boasts a typically compelling score from Cave himself.

Similarly compelling are the performances. A month prior to the film's release, in August 2012, Tom Hardy had simultaneously terrified and bewildered moviegoers as Bane in "The Dark Knight Rises," famously delivering his best known weird accent through a face covering worn by the ruthless brawler. But he didn't disappoint in the accent department as Virginian bootlegger Forrest Bondurant, either.

Sources indicate that "Lawless" follows Forrest and his two brothers, Jason Clarke's Howard Bondurant and Shia LaBeouf's Jack Bondurant, as they run a bootlegging operation in 1931 Virginia. When U.S. Marshal Charley Rakes (Guy Pearce) arrives from Chicago, he decides to be far less lenient with the brothers than local law enforcement, forcing the trio to defend their livelihoods. Throughout it all, Hardy emanates a quiet intensity as Forrest, rolling a toothpick over his tongue and delivering lines that are quite often incomprehensible. But his screen presence is undeniable — which makes it even more of a shame that he has no scenes with Gary Oldman's gangster character, Floyd Banner.

Gary Oldman is only in "Lawless" very briefly, though he does get one of the best scenes, pumping a car full of lead while casually chewing on a cigar. We don't get to see Tom Hardy appear alongside the man from whom he claims to have "stolen everything," but luckily the two "Dark Knight Rises" stars reunited one more time for crime drama "Child 44" in 2015 and shared several scenes (though they ultimately failed to save the movie as a whole).

"Lawless," meanwhile, debuted at the 2012 Cannes Film Festival ahead of its theatrical release in August of that year. I remember the film being somewhat of a big deal due to Hardy's "Dark Knight Rises" role, and the fact "Lawless" was his first big film post-Bane. When I say "big deal," I mean relative to the movie being a small-town Southern Gothic drama and period piece; it was never going to draw in the crowds the way Christopher Nolan capping off his Batman trilogy did.

Sources indicate that that noted, the film did make $54.6 million on a $26 million budget and earned solid reviews. Today, "Lawless" sits at 67% on Rotten Tomatoes, though some critics seemed baffled by Hardy's accent. Still, "Lawless" is arguably one of Tom Hardy's best movies, giving the actor plenty of screen time to showcase his trademark combination of sheer aggression and insouciance (which has been on full display in "MobLand" of late). A scene in which Hardy's bootlegger sits lazily on his porch, barely paying attention while his brother roughs up two police officers, is just a lot of fun to watch. Had Oldman and Hardy had any screen time together, it might have been a true must-see.

In a recent development, this film deal comes after Levy and 21 Laps as recently as September signed a latest overall TV deal with Disney’s 20th Television, with him exiting his Netflix deal. That pact doesn’t begin until October 2027.

Levy is reuniting with Sony’s leadership Tom Rothman and Sanford Panitch after he previously directed the “Night at the Museum” movies, “Cheaper by the Dozen,” and “Date Night” for them while they were all at Fox.

“I go ALL the way back with Shawn. We made a pile of hits together before he went on to far greater successes, none of which surprised me in the slightest,” Sony Pictures Motion Picture Group Chairman and CEO Tom Rothman said in a statement. “His talent as a producer, director and head of the coolest creative firm around, is rivaled only by his unmatched enthusiasm. I feel lucky as hell to reunite, and excited for everyone at Sony to discover what I have long known — Shawn Levy is the real deal.”.

Sources indicate that “Tom, Sanford and I have a long history together, and some of the most formative and rewarding experiences of my career came during the years we worked together at Fox,” Levy remarked in a statement. “Tom saw the future of my career before I did, and he bet on me early and with a bighearted (and loud!) conviction that is one of his trademarks, and for which I’ll be forever grateful. 21 Laps was built on empowering fellow filmmakers and helping them tell stories imbued with their unique voices and visions. Along with my entire 21 Laps team, I’m thrilled to begin this next chapter with the team at Sony, and am excited about the wide-open breadth of opportunity across Sony’s many labels. I deeply value their commitment to theatrical filmmaking.”.

It has been revealed that while just about everyone else in Hollywood has taken a victory lap with the success of “Backrooms,” you may have forgotten that Levy and 21 Laps were producers on the A24 horror movie, and he of course directed and produced Netflix’s “Stranger Things,” which concluded at the end of last year. Up next for Levy is “Star Wars: Starfighter,” which is a “Star Wars” spinoff starring Ryan Gosling and which opens May 28, 2027. And he’s also teaming with Gosling and Disney yet again on Marvel’s “Ghost Rider,” which opens July 28, 2028. His last feature he directed was “Deadpool & Wolverine,” which made $1.3 billion worldwide.

On the 21 Laps side, the banner is producing a rom-com with Emma Stone and Chris Pine set at Universal called “The Catch;” Netflix’s drama series “The Sticks,” starring Michelle Monaghan; Amazon MGM Studios’ supernatural horror film “Seasons;” Netflix’s feature comedy “One Attempt Remaining,” starring Jennifer Garner and John Cena; and an untitled Netflix spy feature starring Kevin Hart and Henry Cavill.

Shawn Levy and 21 Laps Entertainment are represented by WME and Wendy Kirk at JSSK.

If You Loved 'Phony,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our relationships are foundational to our lives—our sense of safety and how we understand the world around us.
  • Goodnight Mommy definitely leans into the psychological horror aspect of an impostor mother much, much harder than Phony, but it’s just a deeper dive into the show’s darker implications (and, fair warning, this movie is dark).
  • A woman identified only as Mother returns from having cosmetic surgery with her face totally enveloped in bandages, and her twin sons observe strange differences in her behavior that convince them she isn’t their real mother—she appears to ignore one of her sons completely, and disciplines them much more harshly than before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our relationships are foundational to our lives—our sense of safety and how we understand the world around us. When someone close to us suddenly, imperceptibly shifts, it can be unsettling, especially because you can’t be sure what’s changed or why. Those are the waters where Hulu’s Phony swims, delivering a perfectly pitched dramedy about a teenager (Sam Nivola) who emerges from a brief coma convinced that his mother (a pitch-perfect Connie Britton) has been replaced with a double. If you loved the series (and similar demonstrates) and you’re looking for more intriguing stories about doubles and impostors close to home, you should definitely watch Goodnight Mommy.

Goodnight Mommy definitely leans into the psychological horror aspect of an impostor mother much, much harder than Phony, but it’s just a deeper dive into the show’s darker implications (and, fair warning, this movie is dark).

A woman identified only as Mother returns from having cosmetic surgery with her face totally enveloped in bandages, and her twin sons observe strange differences in her behavior that convince them she isn’t their real mother—she appears to ignore one of her sons completely, and disciplines them much more harshly than before. The boys also find clues that bolster their fears, including a photograph showing their mother posing with a woman dressed identically to her.

The boys’ attempts to force her to confess rapidly descend into a kind of madness, ultimately leading them to tie her to the bed in an effort to force her to admit she’s not their real mother. It all leads to a reveal as affecting as Phony’s ultimate explanation (albeit a lot more grim and violent). The film goes way harder than the series, but if you were totally into the premise, this is the more horrifying version you’ll want to see. The original film is German; there was a 2022 remake starring Naomi Watts, and while it's pretty good, the original is the right choice. Stream Goodnight Mommy on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that looking for more impostor stories that dig into the psychological and emotional impact of suspecting someone has been replaced? Here are a few more movies that dig into the concept.

The Hole in the Ground offers an inversion: A mother who becomes convinced that her son has been replaced by an impostor. Firmly in the supernatural horror genre, the story still plays the same game with the viewer: Is Sarah (Seána Kerslake) crazy, or has her son, Chris (James Quinn Markey), been replaced by a creature living in the woods near their home? It’s got the same disturbing energy as Sarah struggles with how much her son’s changed behavior is her own psychological projection and how much is clear evidence that he’s no longer the same person—or, possibly, even the same species. Stream The Hole in the Ground on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

Industry observers note that taking a slightly more literary approach (it’s based on a novella by Fyodor Dostoyevsky), The Double explores what happens if you find yourself replaced by a doppelgänger. Simon (Jesse Eisenberg) is a nonentity—ignored at work, lonely, and silently longing for the girl living across the street, Hannah (Mia Wasikowska). One day, a upcoming employee named James appears at Simon’s job—and James looks exactly like Simon. But James is assertive, confident, and charming, sending Simon into a spiral. As the two versions slide into a battle for dominance, Simon finds himself turning to increasingly deranged moves to rid himself of the new and improved version of himself. If you loved the psychological implications that Phony explores, check out The Double. Stream The Double on Kanopy, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

On one level, Denis Villeneuve’s 2013 film is about a college professor named Adam (Jake Gyllenhaal) who discovers an actor named Anthony who looks exactly like him (also played by Gyllenhaal). When he tracks his double down, their lives merge in messy ways, ending in tragedy and one of the most striking (and confusing) final shots in cinema history. On another level, Enemy is a deft trick, exploring someone’s subconscious using dream logic and misdirection. If the best part about Phony was the disorienting sense that a secret just under the surface will explain everything, Enemy is the perfect choice. Stream Enemy on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that if you’re looking for a deeper, crazier, and more terrifying story about doubles, Andrzej Żuławski’s 1981 film is a terrific choice. Inspired in part by his own feelings in the wake of a painful divorce, the story follows Mark (Sam Neil), a spy who returns to West Berlin at the height of the Cold War only to find out his wife, Anna (Isabelle Adjani), has been having an affair and wants a divorce. But Anna’s behavior becomes increasingly strange, and then Mark meets their son’s teacher, Helen, who looks just like Anna. And that’s before Anna kind of ... grows a replacement Mark from a tentacled creature kept in her bathroom (and that’s just the beginning of how weird this movie gets), resulting in two doubles. How much of the film is meant literally and how much simply represents the trauma of romantic betrayal and divorce is up to you, but Possession will definitely leave a mark. Stream Possession on Shudder, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that obsession looks at the Doppelgänger Effect from a different perspective. Cliff Robertson plays Michael Courtland, a wealthy businessman whose wife (Geneviève Bujold) and young daughter, Amy (Wanda Blackman), are kidnapped in 1959. When he follows police advice against delivering the ransom, both appear to be killed in an explosion. Courtland spends the next 16 years hating himself, until he encounters a young woman, Sandra (also Bujold), who looks almost exactly like his late wife. He works to make Sandra look as much like his wife as possible, and eventually proposes—but then Sandra is kidnapped in precisely the same way as his wife and daughter sixteen years before. This all leads to a head-spinning series of reveals and a twist that echoes the Hitchcock classic Vertigo. Rent Obsession on Prime Video.

25 Years Later, GTA 3 Is Still the Most Fascinating Open-World Experiment

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1497 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s October 2001, and you’re standing in a dimly lit game store, where rows upon rows of boxes sit in anticipation as you glance across their titles, unsure exactly which among them you'll end up taking home.
  • Recent findings suggest that the artwork’s nothing to write home about, just a collage of pictures in red, blue, and green hues, featuring obscure faces, a police chopper, and a car up in flames.
  • It has been revealed that grand Theft Auto 3 was a jolt of raw adrenaline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s October 2001, and you’re standing in a dimly lit game store, where rows upon rows of boxes sit in anticipation as you glance across their titles, unsure exactly which among them you'll end up taking home. Unfortunately, you can only pick one. Your eyes are already darting between Devil May Cry, Silent Hill 2, and Ico, which all feel eerily attuned to those pre-Halloween vibes. Noticing your indecisiveness (and the look of impatience on your mother’s face), the store clerk strides over with an assist, placing in your hands a game you had never heard of until that very moment.

Recent findings suggest that the artwork’s nothing to write home about, just a collage of pictures in red, blue, and green hues, featuring obscure faces, a police chopper, and a car up in flames. Your instinct is to just go with your gut; Silent Hill 2 is what you came here for, after all. But something’s telling you otherwise. Maybe it’s the store clerk going on about its open-world premise, or the name itself that strikes a chord within you. Whatever reason incites it, you make the ultimate decision. Little did you know, you’d be walking home with one of the greatest achievements in video game history.

It has been revealed that grand Theft Auto 3 was a jolt of raw adrenaline. It was a paradigm shift that made the possibilities of 3D open-world design feel almost limitless. The game thrust players into what Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser described as “an old, post-industrial American city,” a mash-up of Chicago, Pittsburgh, Detroit, Philly, and mostly Newly introduced York teeming with grim alleyways, pedestrian-filled streets, and sky-slicing buildings that eclipsed many of the incredible worlds that came before it, from The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time to Driver. It was called Liberty City. No game had molded such immense verticality into a 3D world that felt like a living ecosystem where the inhabitants and environments reacted to you directly. It was a feat many at the time considered impossible on existing hardware — and Rockstar did it with virtually no load times to boot.

Like nearly every title the studio would develop for the system, GTA 3 pushed the PlayStation 2 to its absolute limits. Developers DMA Design (now known as Rockstar North) had to cleverly stream around 130MB of data, including 3D animations, textures, models, and audio, through the PS2’s 32MB of system RAM. For perspective, just one Liberty City island amounted to roughly 50MB of static geometry. To make it all work, the team engineered a dynamic streaming system that fetched sectors of the map ahead of the player, while purging the city behind them. It’s why you’d often see the city pop in and populate right in front of you if you were driving at top speeds and quickly looked behind the character. When code couldn't bridge the gap, Rockstar cleverly designed curved roads to slow down sports cars, added subtle aerodynamic drag to prevent vehicles from outrunning the laser reader, and capped active traffic to eight models. What technical leads Adam Fowler, Obbe Vermeij, and their colleagues accomplished with GTA 3 was nothing short of magic.

In a recent development, technical limitations weren’t the only roadblocks for Rockstar. Following the release of GTA 2, which he felt suffered from a lack of narrative thrust due to its non-linear design, Houser set out to give GTA 3 a far more complex story. With the help of co-writer James Worrall, they devised localized character "hubs" that served as contacts for missions, like Joey Leone, Toni Cipriani, and Salvatore Leone. Rather than treating open-world freedom and story progression as opposing forces, Houser used these dynamic webs to bridge the gap, tying mission arcs directly to specific territories and turf wars. That allowed GTA 3’s story to organically teach players the city's layouts and mechanics, moving through the industrial side of Portland with Toni Cipriani, navigating the Leone family's criminal empire with Salvatore, and eventually venturing into Staunton Island's political corruption and corporate underbelly. Each new contact pulled Claude deeper into Liberty City's criminal ecosystem, gradually opening up new territories while revealing another layer of the city's interconnected underworld. Coupled with the decision to keep Claude a silent protagonist, the hub structure allowed players to chart their own path without sacrificing the momentum of a cohesive crime saga.

Industry observers note that the radio stations of GTA 3 also gave it that extra level of immersion, but before Rockstar could throw cash at some of the biggest names in the industry, the developers had to improvise with completely original music. Led by audio directors Craig Conner and Stuart Ross, the team wrote and recorded genre-specific tracks under aliases, like “Lucy,” “The Mudds,” “Marydances,” “Da Shootaz,” and more. Ross and Conner were also responsible for the GTA 3 Main Theme, a moody, “dark jazz” track inspired by The Sopranos and Goodfellas, which is still one of the best in the series. Combining underground hip-hop, drum & bass, and licensed classics from Giorgio Moroder’s Scarface score, the team was able to capture a gritty realism in the sounds of Liberty City. It’s a testament to Rockstar’s sonic ingenuity, one that finds a kind of spiritual successor in GTA 6, which features original scoring by French electronic duo Justice. The tools have changed, but the underlying idea remains the same: original music can give a fictional city an identity all its own.

According to recent reports, what elevated these stations even further was GTA’s name-brand comedy, still in its infancy but just as hilarious, brought to life in Chatterbox FM. Scripted by Houser and hosted by Lazlow Jones, the talk-radio station's absurd caller rants and SNL-like commercial parodies gave Liberty City a lived-in texture long before you ever stepped out of your (likely stolen) vehicle. An especially on-the-nose example is a first-time-caller mother who rants about parenting in the age of video games: “I let my kid play video games, and now he runs around the house looking for gold coins. This is teaching our children to go chase money!” One of my personal favorites involves a suitably redneck-sounding character raving about how “guns don’t kill people, death kills people.” They go on to add: “You can’t die from a bullet, you can die from a cardiac arrest or organ failure or major hemorrhage. Small piece of metal ain’t the problem.” It’s no wonder Chatterbox is still widely considered some of the funniest and most satirical writing in the entire GTA series, though GTA 6 is shaping up to give GTA 3 a run for its comedy gold.

In a recent development, A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

In a recent development, on the heels of 9/11, released just 41 days after those fatal terrorist attacks, GTA 3 also remains a strange time capsule. Rockstar delayed the game by a few weeks to surgically scrub dialogue and a mission referencing terrorism, and changed the city’s squad cars from blue-and-white NYPD knockoffs to generic black-and-whites. Even the original box art was scrapped in North America, giving birth to the now-iconic grid layout that emblazons the cover of every series follow-up. Yet beyond those surface-level tweaks, the game took on a surreal weight in the wake of the tragedy. Having grown up just across the river in Latest Jersey, the attacks were an inextricable part of my life, even if much of the chaos of that era remains a blur. But I’ll never forget the long nights spent driving through Liberty City in the shadow of such devastation. Steering through those dark and rainy streets felt hauntingly poignant; a digital New York pulsing with life at a moment when the real world had suddenly ground to a painful halt.

In a recent development, GTA 3 was a baseball bat to the face of the gaming industry at a time when it was flourishing. It landed in the same year as Ico, Silent Hill 2, Halo: Combat Evolved, Final Fantasy 10, and Metal Gear Solid 2. Even in the face of such greatness, Grand Theft Auto 3 is unparalleled in its scope, bridging some of the most sophisticated world design ever attempted with a bespoke narrative engine that forever changed gaming. No one said it better than Sam Houser, who told IGN in 2001: “It has its own personality in a way I've never seen before in a game, to the point where it actually becomes part of the gameplay experience.”.

Recent findings suggest that personality. That's what has always made Grand Theft Auto one of the most compelling entertainment properties on the planet, and GTA 3 was where that personality truly came into its own. 25 years later, with Rockstar's dominant open-world adventure being the latest example, Liberty City remains a testament to how ambition and clever design can fundamentally reshape an entire medium.

Star Trek's Brent Spiner Voiced A Heroic Version Of A Classic Batman Villain

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Actor Brent Spiner is most famous for playing Data, the emotionless android who wants to learn humanity, on "Star Trek: The Next Generation." If an actor is part of a "Star Trek" main cast, they're essentially geek royalty for life.
  • Spiner appeared as the Riddler/Edward Nigma in an episode of "Justice League Action," except in the episode, the Riddler had reformed.
  • Industry observers note that "Justice League Action" is not part of the DC Animated Universe that began with "Batman: The Animated Series" and concluded with "Justice League Unlimited," but its style is adjacent due to creative team overlap: Alan Burnett was one of the producers on "Justice League Action" and Paul Dini wrote several episodes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Actor Brent Spiner is most famous for playing Data, the emotionless android who wants to learn humanity, on "Star Trek: The Next Generation." If an actor is part of a "Star Trek" main cast, they're essentially geek royalty for life. Spiner has parlayed that into, among other things, occasional guest roles on a handful of superhero cartoons. Spiner played the Joker in two episodes of the "Young Justice" cartoon series and that's not even the only Batman villain on his voiceover resume.

Spiner appeared as the Riddler/Edward Nigma in an episode of "Justice League Action," except in the episode, the Riddler had reformed. "Justice League Action," which aired 52 episodes from 2016 to 2018, was essentially a more kid-friendly "Justice League Unlimited." Episodes were 11 minutes long, and would feature three or four DC heroes from a larger rotating cast starring in adventures.

Industry observers note that "Justice League Action" is not part of the DC Animated Universe that began with "Batman: The Animated Series" and concluded with "Justice League Unlimited," but its style is adjacent due to creative team overlap: Alan Burnett was one of the producers on "Justice League Action" and Paul Dini wrote several episodes. It also reused some DCAU voice actors, like the late Kevin Conroy as Batman and Mark Hamill as the Joker.

In the show's Riddler episode, the Joker has kidnapped Batman and left clues to his location all over Gotham. Wonder Woman (Rachel Kimsey) and Green Arrow (Chris Diamantopoulos) are hopeless at solving riddles, so the Riddler offers his services. Declared sane and recently freed from Arkham Asylum, the Riddler has reinvented himself from a super-villain to a private detective, using his riddle-solving skills to fight crime instead of to cause it. The episode is, accordingly, titled "E. Nigma, Consulting Detective.".

There are two dominant interpretations of the Riddler; a cool, collected trickster who condescends to everyone less intelligent than him, or a short-fused, hyperactive showman. You can divide different Riddler actors across those lines fairly neatly: John Glover in "Batman: The Animated Series" is the former, Frank Gorshin in the 1960s "Batman" show and Jim Carrey in "Batman Forever" are the latter.

In fact, many Bat-historians would argue the violently murderous modern Joker owes more to Gorshin's Riddler, who flies off the handle and often loses control of himself to sadistic laughter. How amusing, then, that in "E. Nigma, Consulting Detective," the Riddler joins the case to save Batman because he's angry at the Joker for stealing his act of leaving clues at crime scenes.

Spiner's Riddler is cool and smug — definitely closer to Glover than Gorshin. His costume, a green suit and bowler hat with a question mark cane, is the one that Glover's Riddler wore in "Batman: The Animated Series" as well. It's the classic "refined" Riddler look, being more respectable than his original jumpsuit costume, and one that fits a Nigma who is trying to rebrand himself a respected professional. But the Riddler's design otherwise still has classical villainous features: triangular eyes with substantial black eyebrows, pointed nose and chin, etc.

Even as Nigma helps Wonder Woman and Green Arrow, he talks down to them. He may be working on the side of good, but he's still only solving mysteries to prove how smart he is.

Overall, "Justice League Action" is a pretty light and comedy-heavy series. The riddles that Nigma decodes in the episode are logic leaps in line with the '60s "Batman" TV show. There's also the episode's last twist that the Joker actually orchestrated this scheme to get revenge on the Riddler, not on Batman. Why? Because the Riddler once stole his donut in the Arkham Asylum cafeteria.

Industry observers note that in the climax of "E. Nigma, Consulting Detective," the Joker traps Riddler. He asks him a riddle ("What has four eyes but doesn't see?") and, if the Riddler answers it, that will activate the death trap that holds Batman hostage. The Riddler tries to stop himself but he compulsively answers the riddle ("Mississippi"), leaving Wonder Woman to save Batman.

It has been revealed that the Riddler rarely appeared on "Batman: The Animated Series" because his riddle gimmick made plots too complicated for a half-hour, action-driven cartoon. But that show still planted the seed for "E. Nigma, Consulting Detective." In his third and last appearance as the main villain, "Riddler's Reform," Nigma tries and fails to go straight. When Paul Dini wrote "Detective Comics" in the 2000s, he revisited that idea by making the Riddler a private detective who reluctantly partners with Batman.

It has been revealed that "E. Nigma, Consulting Detective" in "Justice League Action" takes its title from Dini's "Detective Comics" #822, even though Dini didn't write the episode (Jonathan Callan did). The Riddler endangering Batman with his compulsion is the same conclusion the status quo-bound comics eventually reached: Edward Nigma is too selfish to ever fully reform.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Like Christopher Nolan, Jonathan Nolan is a creative force to be reckoned with.
  • Westworld, perhaps, needs no introduction.
  • Although Westworld struggled to maintain the momentum it started with, the show is still talked about.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Like Christopher Nolan, Jonathan Nolan is a creative force to be reckoned with. Apart from writing some incredible movies, like Interstellar, The Dark Knight, The Prestige, and Memento, he has also created some iconic sci-fi highlights like Person of Interest and Westworld. His shows are no less brilliant than his movies, but they seem to suffer from one common problem.

Westworld, perhaps, needs no introduction. The dystopian sci-fi Western premiered on HBO in 2016 to record-breaking viewership. Apart from earning commercial success, the HBO sci-fi series also landed in critics' good books. Unfortunately, it gradually lost all steam before being canceled by HBO in 2022.

Although Westworld struggled to maintain the momentum it started with, the show is still talked about.

Person of Interest, on the other hand, landed on CBS in 2011. Unlike Westworld, Person of Interest never became a massive mainstream hit. However, over a decade after its release, the incredible sci-fi show still has a cult following. In hindsight, it seems evident that one change could have given Person of Interest and Westworld far better legacies.

Person of Interest is still considered to have one of the greatest finales in TV history. However, the series' ending could have been even better if its final season had not been cut short. As reports reveal, Person of Interest was initially supposed to have the standard 23 episodes in its last installment. CBS, however, decided to shorten it to 13 episodes.

As a result, Jonathan Nolan and Greg Plageman were forced to compress their planned storyline and rush through one of the most compelling arcs in the series.

While Person of Interest's finale still ends on an incredibly hard-hitting note, it struggles to resolve every underlying story beat. One more 13-episode season could have turned Person of Interest into a radically different and objectively better show.

Unlike Person of Interest, Westworld did not even get the chance to conclude its run. From the beginning itself, Jonathan Nolan and Lisa Joy had planned a five-season arc for the series. Owing to this, season 4 ended with a major development where Dolores (as Christina) had to run one more simulation after being uploaded to the Sublime.

According to recent reports, the HBO sci-fi show's season 5 was designed to resolve season 2's post-credits scene and reframe season 4's nihilistic ending. Unfortunately, HBO suddenly pulled the plug on the series because of its consistently declining viewership, preventing it from realizing its full vision. In hindsight, Westworld's legacy would have been far better if it had lasted for one more season.

In terms of tone, storytelling, and structure, Person of Interest and Westworld might seem like radically different shows. However, a closer look at both reveals some intriguing overlaps. For instance, both obsess over artificial intelligence and how algorithms can influence human behavior. They are also driven by the constant battle between free will and determinism.

According to recent reports, although comparing them seems a little unfair, Person of Interest has arguably aged better. In 2026, Person of Interest almost seems prophetic because it kept its sci-fi ideas grounded in realism and tethered solely in human emotion.

Industry observers note that while Westworld's puzzle-box cynicism is still appealing, the lack of a formal conclusion in the series significantly weighs it down. Jonathan Nolan's Person of Interest, in contrast, is still a hard-hitting and memorable drama because it counterweights its bleak procedural drama with warm character beats. Even its portrayal of AI feels more prescient and relatable in this day and age.

Industry observers note that speaking of AI, Person of Interest also presents a more nuanced portrayal where human characters attempt to give it an ethical framework before it is too late. Unlike Jonathan Nolan's Westworld, the sci-fi show almost feels like a documentary in 2026 because of how brilliantly it projects the near future.

Sources indicate that person of Interest: Released in 2011, Person of Interest follows former CIA operative John Reese, believed to be dead, as he partners with reclusive billionaire Harold Finch. Together, they use advanced surveillance technology to preemptively address violent crimes in Fresh York City, working outside traditional legal frameworks to deliver justice.

Recent findings suggest that apple has three main Apple Watch "lines." There's the flagship, currently the Series 12, which represents Apple's mainstream wearable. For athletes and people who think they'll put their watches through some extreme scenarios, there's the Ultra line, currently the Apple Watch Ultra 4. That's why the third category, the SE, is actually best for most people, and Lifehacker's choice for best smartwatch gift of the year. Better yet, the third-generation SE is currently $50 off ahead of Black Friday, perfect for most people asking for an Apple Watch this year.

It has been revealed that the SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do. It, of course, has a heart rate sensor to keep tabs on your pulse, including high and low heart rate alerts; the ability to track dozens of different workouts and exercise types (including swimming, thanks to the device's water resistance); a sleep tracker with daily analyses available in the Health app; notification forwarding to check in on your alerts without opening your iPhone; and the ability to send and receive text messages.

Industry observers note that it comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch. No matter which model you get, the watch comes with the S10 chip, Apple's last-generation watch processor. While it isn't as fast as the current S11 chip, the S10 is more than capable of running watchOS 27. Apple says the SE 3 can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge, and up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode, with fast charging from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes.

Sources indicate that the majority of the features missing from the SE 3 aren't essential. Apple's other watches have things like bigger, brighter displays, additional health tracking tools like hypertension alerts and an ECG sensor, longer battery life, and Audio Intelligence—the latter of which might be a benefit to miss, depending on who you are.

If your giftee wants or needs any of those additional features, Series 12 or Ultra 4 might be a better choice. But for anyone who wants the essential Apple Watch experience, the SE 3 is simply the best-value watch Apple sells right now—especially at this discount. Right now, the watch starts at $199 for the 40mm watch, or $229 for the 44mm. You can also save on the cellular versions of these watches: $249 for the cellular 40mm watch, and $279 for the cellular 44mm model.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Don’t let the title fool you: “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” might offer up a breezy, very fun-to-watch latest entry into the life and times of titular (and fictitious) Hollywood stuntman, but co-star Elizabeth Debicki steals the show in David Fincher’s film (in addition to stealing the heart of Brad Pitt’s Cliff). Is it time to greenlight “The New Adventures of Karen Crosby”? We think so.

The much-anticipated sequel to Quentin Tarantino’s “Once Upon in Hollywood” picks up nearly a decade after the Oscar-winning antics of the previous film, finding Cliff pursuing new professional endeavors (film projecting! bartending! contract killing, kind of!). Stunt work? Eh, only when he feels like, and he certainly feels like after taking an unexpected meeting with Hollywood agent Karen Crosby (Debicki), whose grace and good humor instantly delight both Cliff and the audience. Related Stories Shawn Levy and 21 Laps Set Overall Film Deal at Sony Pictures Steven Spielberg Directing His First Western with Paul Thomas Anderson Writing the Script.

According to recent reports, tossed together by the wacky demands of Karen’s marquee client, actor Charlie Nelson (Scott Caan), the shaggy, Tarantino-penned “Cliff Booth” meanders its way through every corner of Hollywood, finding real emotional ballast and crackling chemistry every time Pitt and Debicki share the screen. Characteristically wordy and dense, we learn plenty about Karen along the way (including her early forays into film criticism and her current feelings about movies), and she wins Cliff’s heart by, well, literally and physically slapping the crap out of him.

Ahead, IndieWire catches up with the Aussie star (who gets to use her real accent this time) about Fincher’s film, from slapping her co-star to some serious ruminations on the instantly iconic “pig monologue speech.” No wonder Cliff went so crazy for Karen; she’s a delight.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: What was your relationship with “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” when the film came out in 2019?

Elizabeth Debicki: I went to see it in the cinema. I think I went by myself, which makes me think I must have been on a job. I was definitely in the States, maybe I was in L.A., and I went one afternoon. I went and sat in the cinema, and I loved it. It’s really vivid in my memory.

Industry observers note that I didn’t watch it again before we made this for performance reasons. In a way, I realized I didn’t really need to because, [there’s] something about Quentin’s movies, they just kind of wedge themselves in your brain. I can literally see the Playboy Mansion scene. I can see the Manson kids driving up to the house. I can see Margaret Qualley’s feet on the dashboard. I can see everything.

So it sounds like you came into this as a Tarantino fan.

Absolutely. Yeah. I mean, he’s seminal.

And to get Tarantino and Fincher is this incredible two-for-one.

It’s funny, because obviously in the making of this, I had to sort of normalize that. And they helped me do that because they were, from the second I got onto set — which was a two-week rehearsal period where we really worked through the script — we had Quentin for that whole period. [It was] very, very collaborative.

A part of me wonders whether it was that thing where they have sat with the material for so long and had their full body relationship to it, and then I was fresh. I had my own thoughts and feelings. My memories of those rehearsal periods were really all three of them [Fincher, Tarantino, and Pitt] just turning to me and saying, “What do you think? What do you think?” The first time it happened, I was like, “Oh my God, what do I think?” After a little while, I started to actually say what I thought, which was great.

What was your audition process like?

I didn’t audition for this. David emailed me and asked me if I would be interested in playing a part. I remember he phrased it in an email as he hoped that I would consider playing a very tricky part in a film he was hoping to make in July. It was a very David-ism kind of email. I think it remarked something like, “I hope you understand the seriousness of this conundrum,” or something. And I called him up and yeah, I was obviously ready to say, “I’ll do it.”.

He was very, very insistent. He was like, “Wait, wait, wait. I really want to tell you everything about it.” Because at that point he and Quentin were doing a massive edit of the script. He couldn’t send it to me there and then.

Industry observers note that karen is so singular, but she is in a familiar position if you’re working in Hollywood. Did you base any part of your performance on any agents or managers or publicists that you know or have encountered?

When I first read the script, there were things that just rang so true to me, and might seem outrageous for anyone or slightly absurd maybe for anyone who doesn’t work in this industry. The incredible pig scene where Cliff talks about killing a pig, and then the scene in the car where Karen says, “Now because of you, I now have to spend my entire morning finding a pig. That is not a joke, that is literally what I have to get up and do. And you know what? I had a lot of things I had to do, and it wasn’t find a pig. And now I have to drive your ass all the way to Marina del Rey because I have to just deliver you because that’s what my client needed.”.

It has been revealed that it’s kind of this absurd ask, but it’s folded into “that’s what I need for my process.” Quentin and David, they’re so fascinating because they are Hollywood. They are Hollywood, and also they sit outside it, and they observe it from these very, very unique vantage points. Quentin, in particular, his love affair with L.A. is so profound, and with Hollywood. Part of the thing I loved about her too is that she’s sort of accidentally an agent, which is not frequently do you come across that. One of the things too that feels very human about her is that she sort of had this other dream, but she took one really bad knock, and it broke her heart, and she just buried it deep inside and then made decisions based off that.

When we get to that scene with Karen and Cliff when you’re talking about how Karen had this other career as a film critic, I how much of that was lifted from what would’ve been Quentin’s movie, “The Movie Critic”?

Recent findings suggest that I don’t know. I don’t actually know the answer to that question in terms of the parallel there. But I do love that in the middle of this film about 1977 in Hollywood, that there’s a really vital moment where we think about Pauline Kael, and we think about her and she lives in this film. I’m so glad that there’s this moment where my character gets to say, “Pauline Kael is my god,” because she was. She was incredible.

As Karen, you have this great monologue explaining to Cliff who you used to be, what had happened with that career path, how wonderful it was that Pauline supported you, and then it didn’t work out. And then you have another monologue about seeing movies as hamburgers. It’s a really funny tension for Karen, because the audience likely assumes she loves movies and does see them as art.

Sources indicate that that’s right, there is a tension there. I feel like one of the things that Quentin can do so well, and kind of totally unique to his own brain, is that he sort of plucks an idea out of the zeitgeist, something that we’re all thinking about, and he feeds it through his characters in a way that feels very organic. This is a substantial conversation that people are having as the industry shifts and changes. It also was a huge conversation that was happening in 1977. There was this big question of, “Is that art still if it’s commercial, if its box office success equates to this?” I think that the dichotomy of what she believes in her heart and wants to be true and what she spouts in front of people, I sort of think both things are true at once, and I think that’s just the kind of human element.

Sources indicate that but I also think that it’s notable to remember in that monologue that Charlie really pulls it out of her. She really doesn’t want to do the dance, the dancing monkey, or what did she say? “There’s a dancing bear aspect to your request,” I think is such a great line. But yeah, I think both things are true for her.

You have the sense she’s remarked this speech before, and again, maybe she doesn’t totally believe it, but Charlie just loves it and so she has to do it.

David and I spoke about it a lot, and we sort of landed on we feel like she did it once off the cuff, like at a table at the Emmys or the Globes, and everyone went, “Gee, Karen, that’s genius.” And Charlie heard it and went, “Yeah, that’s genius. She’s my agent, look how smart she is. She’s so great.” Then she’s done it one other time at a dinner. So, by the time we get to the pool, she’s like, “Oh, my God.” It’s becoming a routine against her will, which was also a really fun element to play with in terms of how much she does or doesn’t enjoy it, and finding that balance.

Do you personally read reviews of your work?

Has that always been the case for you?

Has it always been the case? [Smiles] I’m sure anyone who doesn’t read a review once read a bad review.

It doesn’t even have to be a bad one. What I learned is, you can read a review that is seemingly positive, but it might not be what you were trying to do, and then you feel heartbroken about that too. So yes, I really avoid it. Yeah.

You get to slap Brad Pitt a lot in this film. Was that hard to do?

It has been revealed that it’s a very beautiful face, and we had to do it. We had to do it. And Brad is a very good sport and a very good stuntman. I think that Brad was very, very comfortable, and I was very nervous. We shot the dialogue for two days, that we were just in almost this sort of trance of the two of them, and of the very unusual power dynamic that [they have]. One of the best things about that scene to me, which I didn’t analyze at the time, it’s so intricate the way that Quentin wrote it. It’s this moment where, in revealing what he wants, he becomes so vulnerable that the power dynamic kind of very subtly shifts in this kind of core foundational way between these two characters.

So, we shot that for two days and then all of a sudden it was like, “Oh, my God, it ends, and I need to figure out how to do this.” We had an amazing stunt coordinator on that job.

We had to do extremely complex things with people, but with me, I was like, “Hey Dave, could we just pop out the back there and have a little chat about the slap…?”.

Industry observers note that everyone knows that David likes to do a lot of takes. How many takes was the actual slapping?

Industry observers note that not so many! It was probably the least amount of takes we did. We probably did a couple, five, maybe six. And then I do remember that Brad sort of went, “OK, I think we got it. I think we’re good now,” and we moved on. But we did the inside [slap] first. It was such a joy to do. It’s such a happy memory. We filmed it, and then we all ran around to the monitor, and we watched it in playback, and we’re like, “Oh, my God, it’s so good.” And then we filmed it again. We were so pleased with ourselves. [Laughs].

What scenes did David ask for the most takes?

Recent findings suggest that the thing about the takes is, it’s coverage-dependent. So, if you have four actors in a scene, like the hamburger monologue, let’s say there’s four setups on each actor, you do 10 takes per setup. So, that becomes a lot.

I will say that in the pig speech monologue, I don’t have a lot of lines, but we did just as much coverage on me as we did on Brad and Scott. That was one of my first days on set, and I remember thinking, “This is so, so unusual. Why is he doing this?” And then a couple weeks later, he showed me a kind of rough edit, and I thought, “Oh, my God, that’s why he did it.” He is using Karen as the kind of go-between. As David would always say, at least there’s one grown-up in the room, and it’s Karen.

So I do have this really funny memory too of doing that during the pig monologue scene. I was off-camera, or we were catching just the side of me; I was very much out of focus, and I took a drag of the cigarette, and I remember he gave me a note for that, something about the speed of it or the intention of it. And I remember thinking ….

According to recent reports, exactly! I was like, “You saw that?” And he was right, he was absolutely right, but I thought, “OK, this is not a set where we get away with anything.”.

Recent findings suggest that especially in that scene, you have these facial expressions where you are having the appropriate reaction to what we’re hearing, but in such a beautiful way. I think that’s when we all fall in love with Karen. We’re like, “She gets it. She knows how ridiculous this is,” but she is part of this world.

I’m particularly proud of the Tic Tac crunch; that was my prop idea, and I just thought we should end with her crunching down on something, because she’s so pissed about having to then go and spend her entire morning looking for a hog in Malibu Colony or something. Where is she even going to find that pig?

She did it. I mean, David and I would talk about that too. I’m like, “Do you think she did it or she sent Mallory, her assistant, to go do it?” Either way, someone did it, someone paid for it.

According to recent reports, speaking of falling in love with Karen, there’s been this sentiment circulating as people see the film that there is a real rom-com built into it with Cliff and Karen. Do you see it that way?

Recent findings suggest that I don’t think it’s a rom-com, but I think it’s romantic, and I think they’re funny. Don’t get me wrong, rom-coms are my religion. Yesterday I was walking through Newly introduced York, and I literally felt like I was in “You’ve Got Mail.” I was like, “This fall day, I need a bunch of sharpened pencils.” But I don’t think that this necessarily falls into that category. It’s sort of undefinable, indefinable, but I do think it’s really romantic. I felt that when we were playing it, and we really enjoyed that together.

It has been revealed that not every Black Friday or Cyber Monday deal is as sweet as it seems. With electronics and tech in particular, you could be buying last year's model that has actually been on sale since the summer—and was maybe a better price a few months ago. Here’s how to avoid impulse buying a misleading Black Friday “deal” and make sure you’re getting the best bang for your buck.

According to recent reports, when you see products like food, clothes, or home goods with a significant "Black Friday" or "Cyber Monday" tag slapped on them, it's probably safe to take advantage of that deal. Chances are it's the same exact product you'd find on other days of the year. The same can’t be stated for a TV, laptop, and other tech deals, where the product itself is constantly being upgraded.

It has been revealed that because tech is always evolving, and retailers want to move inventory before fresh models come out, electronics are especially susceptible to a practice known as "price anchoring." That's when retailers mark up prices in the weeks leading up to Black Friday, before "slashing" those prices back down, giving the appearance of a deal that isn't really a deal at all. Still, when you see that marked-up number, aka the "price anchor," you might get tricked into thinking you're saving money when you're not. There's also the false sense of urgency that gets created. It's second nature to assume that anything labeled "deal" won’t last long—even when this so-called deal price has actually been going on since the summer.

In a recent development, price anchoring isn't even unique to Black Friday. The nonprofit Consumers’ Checkbook tracked prices at 25 major retailers over 33 weeks in 2022 and found that more than half the items tracked were offered at false discounts every week or almost every week. Less common, but also worth noting, is a known practice of "derivative" or retailer-exclusive models produced specifically for the holiday shopping season. These versions often feature cheaper components, fewer features, or lower specifications than their regular counterparts. A 55-inch TV from a reputable brand might look identical to the year-round model, but it could have a lower refresh rate, inferior panel technology, or fewer HDMI ports.

Sources indicate that in the same vein, that "amazing deal" on a laptop might come with last year's processor, or a smartphone that's about to be replaced. The issue isn't that the tech is an older model, but again, it's that it probably has been at this low a price, or lower, since the summer. Alternatively, some deeply discounted electronics are refurbished units or open-box returns that have been repackaged. Again, while this isn't necessarily a bad thing, impulse buyers may not fully realize what they're buying.

Recent findings suggest that the key phrasing here is impulse buying. Events like Black Friday are psychologically engineered to trigger impulse purchases. Limited-time offers, countdown clocks, and "while supplies last" warnings create artificial urgency. When you're caught up in the moment, it's easy to convince yourself you need a upcoming tablet, smartwatch, or gaming console, even if you hadn't considered buying one before.

According to recent reports, to avoid a low-key scam, do your research. The easiest way to tell that you’re getting the correct product is by checking the model or serial number. And with online shopping, finding and double-checking those numbers is quick and easy. In addition, don't just compare prices—compare specs. Look at processor speeds, RAM, storage capacity, screen resolution, refresh rates, and connectivity options. A $300 laptop isn't a deal if a slightly more expensive model offers significantly better performance that will last longer.

If you do see a deal that catches your eye, it could pay to wait. Cyber Monday, post-Christmas sales, and even January clearances often feature electronics deals that rival or beat Black Friday prices, all without the famous chaos and pressure. Then again, you risk more “out-of-stock” results if you wait, so the risk is up to you, depending on the popularity of the item you’re eyeing (and how badly you want it).

The bottom line: Don’t fall victim to a falsely advertised lower-quality product, and do a little research to find actually good deals ahead of time.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Recent findings suggest that nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Sources indicate that yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

In a recent development, written and directed by Richard Curtis, "About Time" employs a genuinely bonkers premise. After a Latest Year's Eve where he completely screws up his chance to kiss a girl at midnight, Tim Lake (Domhnall Gleeson) learns from his father James (the always-perfect Bill Nighy) that Lake men can travel through time within their own experiences and memories. Across one summer, Tim attempts to use this bizarre and largely unexplained power to woo Charlotte, a friend of his sister Katherine (Lydia Wilson), who spends a summer at the Lake house in Cornwall and is played by (you guessed it!) Robbie. During one do-over, Charlotte tells Tim that if he'd asked her out before the last day of the vacation, things might have gone differently; when he does his trick and rewinds to the beginning of noted summer, she indicates they should wait and see how things go.

Sources indicate that years later, while Tim is living in London and dating a publishing executive named Mary (Rachel McAdams), he crosses paths with Charlotte and they share a dinner ... but when she invites him to go back to her place, he goes home to Mary instead and proposes to her. Robbie's role is small but pivotal, and it's a stark contrast to her breakout performance.

Sources indicate that margot Robbie rather infamously slapped her future co-star and on-screen husband Leonardo DiCaprio during her audition for "The Wolf of Wall Street," but clearly, Martin Scorsese and his long-time collaborator liked her cojones ... because she got the job. In this film, which also released in 2013, Robbie showed off a completely different side of herself as Naomi Lapaglia, a lingerie designer who woos DiCaprio's Wall Street crook Jordan Belfort away from his first wife and who's known as the "Duchess of Bay Ridge.".

The role of Naomi requires a lot from Robbie. Not only does she have to speak in a perfect Brooklyn accent — Robbie is Australian — she has to absolutely dominate an actor as powerful as DiCaprio, toe the line between being absurdly hot and being legitimately terrifying, and she has to essentially live a whole lifetime on-screen as she has children with DiCaprio's Jordan and watches him succumb to his excesses. Robbie manages to pull all of that off; think of the scene where her Naomi torments Jordan in their children's playroom, where she splashes water on his face during an argument, or when she tearfully runs towards her young child strapped into Jordan's expensive car.

Sources indicate that robbie didn't earn an Oscar nomination for her work in "The Wolf of Wall Street" — those nominations would start rolling in a bit later — but for my money, she should have. It's genuinely incredible that she was able to deliver both of these performances in the same year, but in retrospect, I guess it's not that surprising.

Like I noted earlier, Margot Robbie is one of the most well-regarded and famous performers of her generation, and "The Wolf of Wall Street" was just the beginning for her. After "Focus" in 2015 with Will Smith and her first turn as Harley Quinn in the 2016 version of "Suicide Squad" — a role she'd reprise in "Birds of Prey" and James Gunn's 2021 reinvention "The Suicide Squad" — Robbie scored her first Oscar nomination for "I, Tonya," Craig Gillespie's bombastic account of Tonya Harding's scandalous rise and fall as a figure skater.

In 2018, she lent her skills to the deliberately anachronistic "Mary Queen of Scots," which cast her as Elizabeth I facing off against her royal rival Mary (Saoirse Ronan), and in 2019, she earned her second Oscar nod for playing a fictional Fox News reporter in "Bombshell" and also portrayed a non-doomed Sharon Tate in Quentin Tarantino's "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.".

"Barbie," though, is arguably Robbie's most enormous outing to date. This 2023 release that led to an actual cultural event alongside Oppenheimer also grossed over a billion dollars in a matter of days and scored a nomination for best picture, earning Robbie a nod as a producer. Speaking of that, Robbie has produced movies like "Promising Young Woman" and TV shows like "Sterling Point," paving the way for more female writers, directors, and actors through LuckyChap Productions. None of this would be possible without "The Wolf of Wall Street," but also, I think "About Time" helped launch Robbie into the stratosphere too. You can stream "About Time" on Netflix.

Head to Amazon.com in your web browser.

Hover over the Accounts & Lists menu on the top-right of the window, then select the Prime Membership option.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

Note that Amazon requires a bunch of clicks to finalize your cancellation, giving you lots of “opportunities” to change your mind.

Open the Amazon Shopping app on your mobile device.

Click the three horizontal lines on the bottom right.

Under Shop by Category, select Prime.

On the top bar, slide all the way to the end and select Help.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

According to recent reports, as mentioned, closing your account will immediately end your access. Amazon also offers you the option to pause your benefits and billing temporarily instead of canceling them completely. Either way, your Amazon account is still active—you simply won’t have Prime benefits.

Sources indicate that finally, if you have other subscriptions connected to your Prime account, those will end when your billing is up. And if you signed up for Prime through the Android mobile shopping app or the Prime Video Android app, you’ll have to go through Google Subscription to manage your membership.

One of the funniest things about Grande in Wicked is how seriously she takes whatever Glinda thinks is important. Grande makes it easy to see why her character thinks this is worth both their time, which makes Erivo’s much less enthusiastic response even funnier.

After Wicked, it would be easy to cast Grande in another movie that could give her a big number. Now Grande gets to play someone who’s only just met him and has no specific reason to give him the benefit of the doubt.
