  • Max is a cab driver who’s been telling himself for years that the job is temporary.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that one of Grand Theft Auto 6’s strangest random encounters occurs when you’re offering taxi services, and a man with a beard wearing a dark suit and sunglasses climbs into the backseat with a gun. This can happen if you’re playing as either Jason or Lucia, but both scenes play out the same way: The man wants you to run a red light, ignore phone calls, and drive him to Harborside Park in Vice Beach. He also sounds an awful lot like Tom Cruise, with a calm but forceful demeanor that seems almost sociopathic. Several clips of the sequence have already hit the internet, and to many people, it’s an obvious nod to Collateral, Michael Mann’s 2004 thriller about a hitman who takes a cab driver hostage.

Industry observers note that jason or Lucia gets a better deal than Mann’s cabbie in this Easter egg. If you take the stranger to his destination and follow him inside after he takes out some of the criminals there, you can find a ton of valuable loot. Most players seem keen on eliminating the stranger rather than keep driving him around. In Collateral, Jamie Foxx’s character, Max, has to spend the whole night driving Cruise’s Vincent around Los Angeles. If you’ve never seen how that goes for him, Collateral is streaming for free on Pluto TV — and it’s a must-watch, especially if you want a movie that has a vibe as wild and crime-filled as GTA 6’s.

Max is a cab driver who’s been telling himself for years that the job is temporary. He wants to start his own limo tech giant someday, so when a well-dressed passenger named Vincent (Cruise) offers him $600 to drive him around for the night, it seems like the kind of opportunity that could get him a little closer to quitting. Then a body lands on his cab at their first destination. Vincent has five people to kill before the night is over. Max has just agreed to drive him to all five stops — and he’s already an accomplice.

Vincent is one of Cruise’s best roles because so much of what makes him convincing as an action hero makes him downright scary here. The same certainty that lets Ethan Hunt talk somebody into jumping out of a plane makes it seem perfectly reasonable, for about half a second, when Vincent asks Max to help him stuff a body in the trunk. He’s also an obnoxious backseat driver. The longer he spends in the cab, the more interested he becomes in why Max has seemingly wasted so much of his life. Some of his advice is irritatingly solid, yet he’s also a man who could end the conversation with a single gunshot whenever he wanted to.

It has been revealed that despite the plot focusing entirely on Vincent’s assassinations, Foxx emerges as the real heart of Collateral. Early on, he picks up a prosecutor named Annie (Jada Pinkett Smith), and their conversation has the easy rhythm of two strangers who realize they’d like the ride to last a little longer. You get to see how good Max is at putting people at ease as he flirts a little. Then, Vincent hops in the back, and the nightmare begins. Once the hitman is in the car, even the smallest decisions Max makes​​​​​​​ — like when to look in the rear-view mirror and when to keep his eyes on the road — feel like consequential choices Max must make carefully​​​​​​​.

For a movie about a man on a deadline, Collateral is remarkably willing to pull over and look around. Vincent himself comments early on about how much​​​​​​​ he despises the city’s sprawling, depersonalized atmosphere. Mann often dwells on that atmosphere​​​​​​​ to build up tension. In the movie's best quiet moment, a coyote crosses the road in front of the cab, and both men stop talking to watch it. Los Angeles feels eerie and sinister, lit by flickering streetlights and bland storefronts. As their night continues, even mundane locations feel like the most dangerous places in Los Angeles.

The story’s arc is also immensely satisfying. We see what this pressure cooker does to Max, forcing him to evolve from a passive bystander in his own life to someone who takes an active role​​​​​​​. The evolution is subtle at first as Max resists Vincent’s demands, eventually mustering up the courage to become openly defiant​​​​​​​. Vincent spends the night needling Max about all the chances he’s too scared to take — putting a down payment on a limo, calling Annie since she left him her card, etc. — and by the time they inevitably face off, Max is finally willing to take one.

Sources indicate that GTA 6 so often positions your character as the Vincent of its story, stealing cars and killing people for the next major score. But forcing you to become something closer to Max, at least for a little while, is nothing short of brilliant. The Grand Theft Auto franchise at large owes a great deal of its overall vibe to Mann’s filmography. GTA 5, in particular, is largely inspired by Mann’s 1995 crime film Heat. So it's only fitting that its direct sequel pays homage to another Michael Mann classic — with a little bit of Miami Vice thrown in too, for good measure.

Collateral is available to stream for free on Pluto TV and with a subscription on Paramount Plus.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that fresh off making the best "Spider-Man" movie in about a decade with "Brand Newly introduced Day," director Destin Daniel Cretton is plunging into the Land of Fire and ninjas, adapting Masashi Kishimoto's manga/worldwide phenomenon "Naruto" into a live-action film, two years after it was first confirmed. Translating a battle shonen manga/anime into live-action carries negative associations of past, failed attempts. Why bother moving a story designed to stretch reality's limits to a medium that's inherently more confining than a hand-drawn one? Will "Naruto" break this curse? It has a huge stage to do so, and the early steps look promising.

Deadline has reported that actor Hiroyuki Sanada ("Shogun," "John Wick: Chapter 4") is in negotiations to star in "Naruto" as Hiruzen Sarutobi, the Third Hokage and leader of Naruto's ninja village, Konohagakure. Sanada is the second major actor rumored to be joining "Naruto," after reports in August that Charles Melton had been approached to play Kakashi Hatake, Naruto's masked sensei.

This alone suggests "Naruto" is serious about getting impressive talent: one of the coolest actors alive in Sanada, and a major young actor in Melton, who's won acclaim for his performances in "May December" and "Beef" Season 2. Not for nothing, Sanada and Melton are Japanese and Korean American, respectively — no whitewashing here, so far, contrary to "Naruto" fans' long-standing jokes about Tom Holland or Timothée Chalamet starring as Naruto.

"Naruto" has launched a "global" search/audition process for the movie's three young leads: Naruto and his teammates Sasuke Uchiha and Sakura Haruno. That suggests the film's creators are looking for young actors — possibly, even plausibly, unknowns — who can embody those characters first without prioritizing pre-existing star power.

Casting Hiroyuki Sanada as the Third Hokage suggests the "Naruto" team is already looking to the horizon and seeing sequels. Hiruzen is only a background part of the first "Naruto" arc, "The Land of Waves" (which is the ideal starting place for a movie series). But he takes center stage in the second and third arcs, where one of his former students, the snake-like Orochimaru, serves as the main villain. Hiruzen gets a major action sequence confronting Orochimaru, and casting Sanada — a martial artist who holds a black belt in karate, just as Charles Melton has one in taekwondo — seems like casting with that scene in mind.

Sources indicate that if the goal is adapting the "Naruto" manga as a whole, then forward thinking will be key. The manga runs 700 chapters, divided into several story arcs; you'd likely need somewhere between seven and 10 movies to complete it. The live-action "Naruto" is being produced by studio Lionsgate in partnership with Sony. Lionsgate recently proved once more that "The Hunger Games" is a reliable hit for them with the success of "Sunrise on the Reaping." But it's never smart to put all your eggs in one basket. "Naruto" hits overlapping demographic appeal and even some similar story beats as "The Hunger Games" (like children becoming killers and the tragic horrors of war).

Industry observers note that moreover, comic books have become the prime IP of Hollywood these past two decades, and yet manga outsells American comics many times over. Manga/anime is in the cultural mainstream for anyone younger than a young millennial, and the first studio to crack that could be sitting on a cultural gold mine. So, yeah, Lionsgate has a strong incentive to get "Naruto" right, and the talent it's recruiting suggests they understand that.

Even if Destin Daniel Cretton doesn't stick around for any of those potential "Naruto" sequels (I have to imagine Sony and Marvel Studios want him back for more "Spider-Man" movies), getting him as director for the first is another sign that Lionsgate is taking this seriously. Look at what he's directed, and consider how he's intent on casting actors with genuine martial arts bona fides for "Naruto," and it's clear why he's the man for the job.

An essential part of "Naruto" is its fight choreography, which is more choreographed around hand-to-hand martial arts than most other battle shonen. Yes, the ninjas in "Naruto" use "jutsus," or magical/superpowered attacks powered by spiritual energy, or chakra. But the core of the series' fight scenes is mano-a-mano fights that lay on the brutality and raw emotion; that's especially true in Naruto and Sasuke's various duels.

Sources indicate that the combat in "Naruto" likewise employs parkour acrobatics in the vein of wuxia. (In-universe, ninja learn to channel their chakra to balance on, climb, and run through trees.) Cretton directing "Shang-Chi," a wuxia-flavored Marvel movie, and Spider-Man, who webslings through New York City like how Naruto and his ilk dash through forests, gives him the perfect experience to deliver the heightened-but-not-completely intensity of the action from the early "Naruto" arcs.

Cretton also has the perfect sensei to consult with in Masashi Kishimoto, who has endorsed Cretton as the perfect director for the project, the same way that "One Piece" creator Eiichiro Oda personally approved elements of Netflix's "One Piece" series. "One Piece" proved live-action shonen manga/anime can work in the TV format, and "Naruto" might be the project that proves it can be a blockbuster movie.

"Naruto" is right now in development.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note: This article contains spoilers for “Minotaur.”.

Director Andrey Zvyagintsev has worked with supervising re-recording mixer Andrey Dergachev for 20 years, since the director’s second film, “Banishment.” On each project, including their most recent portrait of a rotten marriage in a rotten world, “Minotaur,” they’ve tried to improve the sound design—using it as a hook that makes the film’s world feel more vital and alive for the audience.

It has been revealed that seriously, spoilers. This is never more true than in the absurdly sad and funny, then suddenly murderous confrontation between cuckolded husband Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov) and his wife’s lover Anton (Yuriy Zavalnyouk) at the hinge point of “Minotaur.” Related Stories Super Bowl LXI to Play Live on IMAX Screens ‘Cliff Booth’ Star Elizabeth Debicki on Slapping Brad Pitt, ‘The Movie Critic,’ and the Rom-Com Question.

According to recent reports, zvyagintsev and Dergachev generally strive to preserve as much authentic production sound from performances as possible. “On my third movie, ‘Elena,’ we recorded the live sound from shooting, and it’s maybe two or three phrases we had to rerecord, but otherwise the whole sound that you hear is fully recorded during the shooting,” Zvyagintsev told IndieWire on an upcoming episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “Our main purpose is to keep as much sound from the shooting as possible and not to add anything extra, and it was the same for ‘Minotaur.’”.

But for the moment that Gleb attacks Anton, and its aftermath, it was crucial to Zvyagintsev that the world beyond the apartment start intruding on Gleb — that even though he wants desperately to cover up what he’s done and make sure no one sees or learns about it, we hear dozens of ways in which he isn’t alone. That required a lot of work outside of the studio to record the background noises Zvyagintsev and Dergachev could then layer into the scene.

“We were creating [background] sounds of the kids playing football in the backyard. We would spend the whole day recording the kids, how they’re speaking, the way they’re playing, people passing by on the street,” Zvyagintsev noted. They also recorded different sound layers from Gleb’s luxury SUV, which they could deploy to create maximum panic in both Gleb and the audience.

“The car signals, the leaves on the street, the birds — they all pronounced, and [emphasized] something. So we were modulating all those layers that we recorded, and then we combined them to create the atmosphere and to put it all in one place for the scene,” Zvyagintsev said.

There’s atmosphere from outside and from inside, as Zvyagintsev and Dergachev refused to let Gleb have a moment of peace on the soundtrack — until, as with all the cruel jokes of “Minotaur’s” filmmaking, he gets it in the worst way, at the worst possible moment. There’s a terrible silence once he’s struck Anton on the head with his own camera. And then the world comes rushing back in, even louder than before.

“We were trying to create this volume of sounds right after the hit. And then, when Anton is falling, there is this complete silence. And then somewhere far away we hear the car alarm and even more sounds that create this volume. This is what we were looking for,” Zvyagintsev mentioned.

It was key to finesse the sound design of the sequence so as not to overplay it. Zvyagintsev initially wanted to add music to the moment, but had to hold himself back. “It was really tempting,” Zvyagintsev remarked. “My composer Evgueni Galperine even wrote the music, which we added. But when we saw the result, we realized, and I understood that no, no, it has to be completely silent.”.

Silent as the grave, one might say. But it’s the sound design, the modulation between loudness and silence, that makes the moment so horrifying. Zvyagintsev and Dergachev did it by hand, just to make sure of it.

“Minotaur” is now playing in select theaters.

#97511. From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2640 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Indiewire ↗ Open Full Page

From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2640 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jimmy Stewart once stated that with movies, it’s key moments that people remember.
  • According to recent reports, emily Blunt, who’s on the circuit these days talking about her standout role as a language-spouting meteorologist in Steven Spielberg’s “Disclosure Day,” gave me some memorable scenes that she will never forget from her wide-ranging filmography.
  • In a recent development, clearly, Blunt can deliver in any genre: romance, comedy, musical, sci-fi, action, thriller, drama.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jimmy Stewart once stated that with movies, it’s key moments that people remember.

According to recent reports, emily Blunt, who’s on the circuit these days talking about her standout role as a language-spouting meteorologist in Steven Spielberg’s “Disclosure Day,” gave me some memorable scenes that she will never forget from her wide-ranging filmography. (We spoke on Zoom.).

In a recent development, clearly, Blunt can deliver in any genre: romance, comedy, musical, sci-fi, action, thriller, drama. So far, Blunt has notched one Oscar nomination, for Supporting Actress in Christopher Nolan’s bio-drama “Oppenheimer.” Sci-fi thriller “Disclosure Day” could score Blunt’s first Best Actress nod. (More below.) Related Stories How Sound Design Helps ‘Minotaur’ Get Away with Murder Super Bowl LXI to Play Live on IMAX Screens.

1. “My Summer of Love” (2005, Pawel Pawlikowski) was Blunt’s first movie role. “I remember the wildness of that Edith Piaf dance [‘La Foule’], where I have the cigarette dangling out of my mouth, and she’s trying to romanticize this girl from the wrong side of town and sophisticate her. I remember the scene with Paddy Considine where she tries to seduce him and then she laughs at him. I will never forget the energy in that room and how Paddy was in that scene. I have taken what Pawel taught me about ambiguity and reality on camera, and I have used it throughout my career. I am an untrained actor. I don’t have anything technical to fall back on, but the aliveness that he created on ‘My Summer of Love’ was informative for how I moved forward: what lies beneath the character. You know what the front foot is, and what is the shadow of that person? What’s really going on?”.

According to recent reports, 2. “The Devil Wears Prada“ (2006, David Frankel) marked Blunt’s Hollywood breakout as Miranda Priestley’s beleaguered first assistant Emily Charlton. After she gets hit by a taxi, second assistant Andy Sachs (Anne Hathaway) visits her hospital room. Charlton is angry and tearful at everything she is missing. “The hospital scene makes me laugh because that’s really who she is: this completely broken down, vulnerable, insecure person.”.

According to recent reports, 3. “The Young Victoria” (2010, Jean-Marc Vallée) gave Blunt a queen to embody. “I remember the scene where she asks [Prince] Albert to marry her, because he was not allowed to ask her. She is the monarch, and had to be the one to ask. That scene was so vulnerable and beautifully twinkly, how Jean-Marc shot that.”.

4. “The Adjustment Bureau,” a romantic sci-fi thriller, co-starred Matt Damon. “I remember never being able to get through a scene with Matt Damon without laughing. But I did love the scene in the bathroom where they meet. That scene had to sparkle because otherwise you don’t care about them, and you don’t care about them using their magical fedoras to get back to each other. Matt Damon doesn’t know how to be bad. That’s the truth. He doesn’t know how to play a false note. There is something about what Matt does, and he’s so dexterous in his humanity, but I don’t feel it’s technical with Matt. He’s like a laser beam of truth, and I feel myself, anyone who watches him, they ease back and they go, ‘Oh, thank God, Matt Damon’s here.’ He just leads with the truth. He’s like Josh Brolin. They only know how to be honest, and so they have such humanity to them. That’s why you can’t take your eyes off them. John [Krasinski] and I were so proud of what Matt did [with “The Odyssey”]. It’s obviously the most Herculean undertaking, but he grounded everything with that performance.”.

Sources indicate that 5. “Edge of Tomorrow” (2014, Doug Liman) co-starred Tom Cruise and thrust Blunt into action mode for the first time. Her moment was a war scene set on a beach. “It was the beach set, and we started calling it ‘the bitch’ because it was such a nightmare. That set was always flooded. You were always exposed to terrible elements of the weather, freezing, and we shot that beach scene for a month. Tom Cruise gave me a lot of flowers on that one. He was so good to me, and he revealed halfway through the shoot that this was the deep end of action for him— this was the most challenging action movie that he had ever done, and it was my first action movie, so I was flung in at the deep end of action. But we held each other through that. I loved athletics when I was a kid, and then couldn’t be bothered to work out, and then thought I knew what working out was, and then I realized I didn’t know what working out was until I started training for ‘Edge of Tomorrow,’ and that was a transformational thing to my body. She needed to look lethal, absolutely lethal. And so it helped me a lot, doing all of that physicality.”.

6. “Into the Woods” (2014, Rob Marshall), adapted from Stephen Sondheim’s stage musical, boasted a huge ensemble cast; Blunt played the baker’s wife opposite James Corden. “‘Moments in the Woods,’ that major song she has right before she gets squished by the giant. She’s weighing up the duality of life, whether she goes for this poetic interlude in her prosaic life or if she goes back to the prosaic life. That kind of agony that she’s going through in the song was cool. I had I’d never sung in front of anyone before, really, other than one small TV thing years ago. I didn’t even want to audition for it, and Rob Marshall said, ‘Look, I’m not looking for singers who can kind of act. I’m looking for actors who can kind of sing,’ and that was great advice. I said it to my 12-year-old this morning as she went off to her musical audition at school. I said, ‘Don’t worry about the notes; just tell us a story. That’s it. That’s what the song should be, and that’s what will make it sound amazing.'”.

According to recent reports, 7. “Sicario” (2015, Denis Villeneuve) plops Blunt’s straight-arrow FBI agent into a violent Mexican border scenario. “The scene that stands out for me is a spellbinding one, when Benicio del Toro comes to my apartment, and he puts the gun to my face and forces me to sign the contract. It’s right at the end of the movie, and I think that scene holds a special place for me because we were not sure about the scene that was written by Taylor Sheridan. It didn’t feel like it belonged in what we were trying to achieve between the characters. We wanted to change it a little bit. It was an idea that Benicio had. We were racking our brains as to how to finish this scene and this moment between the two characters. He always has so many crazy ideas, and he will have some absolute bangers in there. And he called me at about 11 o’clock the night before, and he goes, ‘I think I have it. What about this?’ And I said, ‘That is a great idea, because you’ve got this very idealistic FBI agent who’s pulled into this incoherent, amoral world. And she’s being forced to sign a contract that notes everything they did was aboveboard, and that’s like a death to a character like that.’ We rehearsed that scene for two hours. Denis loved it, and then we all turned to [cinematographer] Roger Deakins: “Roger, what do you think?” And he gave his slow nod of approval, and then we shot it, and it was so.”.

8. “A Quiet Place” (2018, John Krasinski) was Blunt’s first experience being directed by her husband. The memorable moment: giving birth in the bathtub as a killer monster hovers nearby, listening for any noise. “We shot that whole sequence from the water breaking in the bathtub in order, which I was grateful to John for. It took four days. We did two takes of that bathtub scene because he shot it mainly as a oner. It starts as the blood’s trickling out, and it comes up, and you see the creature, and then it goes into that scream, and then the fireworks go off, but yeah, it’s a wild scene. It’s really smart to have a baby in a silent world. Every woman I’ve spoken to about that scene, they go: ‘Oh my God, that scene made me cross my legs.” And I was: ‘Okay, all right.'”.

9. “Oppenheimer” (2023, Christopher Nolan) offered Blunt a constrained role as Kitty, the recessive wife of the great physicist (Cillian Murphy). Blunt agreed that the scene that earned her the Oscar nomination was in the courtroom where she is badgered by the formidable Jason Clarke. “I knew that was the monster scene. When I read the script, I thought, ‘What an extraordinary scene, that you have this person staggering in, looking like a liability,’ and Chris had written that she almost chokes, and you think she’s going to blow it. When I talked to him about it after I read the script, I stated, ‘What a reclamation that scene is of that extraordinary brain coming back to life.’ The brain that had gone crazy at the ironing board, probably meant for bigger things than being someone’s wife and someone’s mummy, and I had a great deal of empathy for her and a lot of women who went crazy at the ironing board. She owns Jason Clarke in a way, and you realize she could probably run circles around him. He played such a wonderful bully in that film, but we saw what Meryl [Streep] did with Miranda Priestley: There’s such power in quiet, great, great power and great dignity.”.

It has been revealed that 10. “The Devil Wears Prada 2” (2026, David Frankel) allowed Blunt to indulge Charlton’s excesses. “We all had scenery stuck in our teeth on that one. It was so fun to go back to playing that lunatic. My favorite scene was the funeral scene where she comes in and rants about Dolce and Gabbana. It was such a ludicrous outfit to be wearing to a funeral. Anne Hathaway is the most unstoppable force. And what a wide range of roles she has access to. I feel this moment in her life. She’s in this full wingspan of being able to harness everything she can do and everything she has to offer, and I can’t believe she had the year she just did, and she was pregnant!”.

Recent findings suggest that “Disclosure Day” (2026, Steven Spielberg) leaned on Blunt to carry the sci-fi thriller. “The four-and a-half minute oner in the beginning when she arrives at the news station. I’ve seen what Steven Spielberg can do visually, his visual prowess is rather unparalleled. So to be in a oner that he conjures up on the day, that happened spontaneously — he was planning on covering it. And I remarked, ‘what would help me so much is if you could let me whirlwind out of control in one take from the moment I pull up, going into the makeup room, coming out speaking Korean, she’s in this incoherent tailspin, and then you see her disintegrate over the course of it. And she gets up there to deliver the weather, and she starts to speak in the alien language. Can we just try it as a oner, just for me to see where I’ve got to get to?’ And he watched me do it. And by the time I got up there to do the weather, my legs were shaking. I was out of breath, beside myself, and he loved it. And he goes, ‘We’re going to do it as a oner.’ And we were done by 2 pm. because he planned to shoot it all day. It was Steven in his element of going, ‘Oh, I see it’ and not only was he intentional about creating the environment for me to be able to do that so he didn’t overcover it, he saw a cinematic advantage.”.

Blunt plays several characters in one. “All the stuff in the childhood home was deeply moving because that also dealt with that moment where the character goes from crisis to serenity and the ability to then deploy these powers rather than be puppeteered by them. So I loved that shape-shift in the character, like playing two people throughout the course of this film. And the other moment that felt so human to me was the panic attack in the box car after the train sequence, and she’s at max capacity, bubbling over, overwhelmed, and a few people, including myself on set, had experienced panic attacks, and that felt like a real reaction to someone who was utterly overwhelmed. That also felt so Spielbergian: no one’s a slick elite action hero in Steven’s films. Everyone’s afraid. Everyone, including Indiana Jones, everyone’s scared. That hand that’s shaking on the way to Omaha Beach, that is trauma. He can relate to your vulnerabilities. Everyone’s a bit over their head, and in a different action movie, me and Josh O’Connor would have dropped in the boxcar and gone, ‘Whoa, that was crazy.’ And instead, she has a panic attack. I got them a lot in my early twenties, and Steven’s not immune, neither is Josh. All of us have experienced that. That moment where he takes my hands and he puts them on the piano and he goes, ‘This is real. This is real. Feel this. I’m here. You’re here. We’re here.’ I’ve done that. So it just was like, ‘Oh my God!’ You get to sublimate what you’ve experienced into this creative art form sometimes. That’s the great gift often on movies.”.

In a recent development, the languages were right in Blunt’s wheelhouse. She has always loved languages. She learned them two to three months before the start of the shoot. “I learned those scenes. The first thing I learned was the Russian and the Korean, because I wanted it to be spoken at such a velocity that it sounded as conversational as it does as me speaking to you right now, and she doesn’t know she’s speaking Russian,” she said. “She thinks she’s speaking English. You have someone who is white-knuckling their way through most of this film, and these forms of mind control are unconscious to her in the beginning, it’s compulsive.”.

Next up: “Walk the Blue Fields” directed by John Crowley and co-starring Andrew Scott as another hot priest, Father Joe, presiding at a wedding. “It’s a short story that I bought the rights to about six years ago by Claire Keegan. If you’ve ever read any of her short stories, they’re like laser beams. They’re so wonderful. My sister Felicity is a book agent. She represents Claire, and she sent it to me. Story A is a wedding day, and story B is what led up to that wedding and why everything is starting to unravel on the wedding day. And it plays like a thriller,” she said. “She’s coming back to Ireland to try to build a relationship with her Irish father [Ciaran Hinds] after they’ve been estranged for years, and it’s a story about identity and religion and love. Andrew Scott has to be one of the most beautiful actors I’ve ever shared a scene with.”.

According to recent reports, and, of course, John Krasinski’s upcoming “Quiet Place 3,” which co-stars Jack O’Connell, Cillian Murphy, Jason Clarke and Noah Jupe, is shrouded in secrecy. “I don’t want to blow John’s cover here,” she said. And “Sicario 3” is also moving forward with the original cast, a script by James Bond writer Steven Knight and director Padraic McKinley.

#97508. 7 Reasons Sunrise On The Reaping Became One Of 2026's Biggest Box Office Successes

7 Reasons Sunrise On The Reaping Became One Of 2026's Biggest Box Office Successes

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1184 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the newest Hunger Games movie, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, hit theaters just last weekend, and already, it's proven to be a smash hit.
  • Recent findings suggest that presently, Sunrise on the Reaping has a very impressive 94% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes—and, notably, its critic score isn't terrible either, currently sitting at 68%.
  • Although there is plenty that worked for the movie in terms of its own merits, there's no question that Lionsgate was wise to release the movie when it did.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the newest Hunger Games movie, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, hit theaters just last weekend, and already, it's proven to be a smash hit. In fact, by Sunday, Sunrise on the Reaping had the fifth-best domestic opening in 2026 so far, and its box office success is only going to grow. Reviews of Sunrise on the Reaping have been a bit mixed, with some finding that the franchise has begun to feel a bit too repetitive or wrapped up in its own lore. However, fans have certainly had a different response.

Recent findings suggest that presently, Sunrise on the Reaping has a very impressive 94% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes—and, notably, its critic score isn't terrible either, currently sitting at 68%. Sure, there have been some complaints from fans, such as changes the movie made to the Sunrise on the Reaping book, but for the most part, it is finding plenty of popularity and success. And, in terms of the latter, these seven aspects of the film (including ahead of its release) in particular helped to make that happen.

Although there is plenty that worked for the movie in terms of its own merits, there's no question that Lionsgate was wise to release the movie when it did. Sunrise on the Reaping managed to avoid some of the trickiest release windows of the year, particularly considering that it opted not to release first over the weekend of Thanksgiving, which is a notoriously difficult time of year for competition between movies.

However, this year, things are a bit different, as Thanksgiving won't be the most competitive period for theatrical releases at all. Rather, that title will undoubtedly go to what is being called Dunesday, December 18, on which both Dune: Part Three and Avengers: Doomsday will be released. Had Sunrise on the Reaping debuted in December, it may very well have run into trouble, but with the release window that was chosen, the movie had an even better chance to thrive.

In addition to a wise release schedule, Sunrise on the Reaping benefited enormously from the marketing for the movie. For months ahead of the release, the cast of the movie were giving various interviews and making myriad appearances, and Maysilee Donner actress Mckenna Grace in particular made the press tour work to her advantage, especially with her decision to consistently wear outfits that were callbacks either to previous red carpets for the franchise or outfits from the other movies themselves.

However, even outside of the cast, marketing for the movie was brilliant, including a chillingly well-timed in-universe ad that played during the United States election night this year and came from President Snow himself. With moves like that, Sunrise on the Reaping was getting quite a bit more attention than is arguably typical of a movie like this.

Recent findings suggest that helping the other more traditional forms of marketing for Sunrise on the Reaping was the use of social media. In fact, Lionsgate itself made great use of social media, making what are effectively fan edits for months, and ultimately turning that into an incredibly popular trailer idea, offering fans the opportunity to make a fan edit that would become an official trailer. In general, though, Sunrise on the Reaping was absolutely everywhere on social media, from Instagram to TikTok and beyond.

That presence from Lionsgate also translated to organic chatter on these myriad social media platforms, with many accounts talking about the books, sharing cast interviews and funny moments, speculating about potential additions to the movie, and more in the months leading up to the film's debut.

There's no question that the movie was massively boosted by the star-studded cast. In addition to the fact that the incredibly popular Mckenna Grace was playing Maysilee, Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy had fans beyond excited, as he is a relatively up and coming actor who has started to have a very dedicated following. However, there were many other major names tied to the project, such as Elle Fanning and Maya Hawke, that had fans eager to see the movie as well.

That, in particular, is actually a very impressive aspect of Sunrise on the Reaping, as it is notoriously difficult to recast beloved characters and actually have it work out. For the most part, though, these fresh actors were met with open arms, and their depictions of the characters ended up being celebrated rather than divisive.

While Lionsgate made many wise decisions and the cast members were absolutely excellent, it shouldn't be overlooked that Sunrise on the Reaping also simply had some incredible source material that gave it the foundation it needed to be successful. All of Suzanne Collins' Hunger Games books have been brilliant, but Sunrise on the Reaping became very popular because of its focus on Haymitch, its ability to weave together elements from the previous books and movies, and the way it didn't shy away from the true brutality of the Capitol.

In a recent development, that alone meant that fans of the franchise were going to make their way to theaters this November, as they knew the story and wanted to see it on the big screen. This, again, is impressive, as this book represented Collins' decision to go back and flesh out a fan-favorite character, which is a risky decision—but, clearly, it totally paid off.

According to recent reports, it's true that Sunrise on the Reaping is a great book, but the fact is, the Hunger Games franchise in general is beloved, and that was also going to offer a guarantee of a certain number of theater-goers. For nearly 20 years now, these characters have been immensely popular, and that arguably means that, no matter what Collins or Lionsgate put out, fans are going to want to see it.

It has been revealed that it helps that the very notion of the Hunger Games franchise is a compelling and, in many ways, topical one, even as it is absolutely horrifying and disturbing. These books and movies have staying power for a reason, and Sunrise on the Reaping was able to build upon that and find so much success in part because of it.

Industry observers note that finally, there's very little doubt that the earlier confirmation that Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson were going to appear in the movie contributed to ticket sales and fan excitement. Already, the epilogue of the novel had revealed that Peeta Mellark and Katniss Everdeen play a role in this story, but that didn't automatically mean that these fan-favorite actors were going to appear.

However, just a few weeks before Sunrise on the Reaping hit theaters, Lawrence gave an interview confirming that they would be making an appearance in the movie, and that led to a massive wave of interest and excitement, especially online, from fans. Granted, Katniss and Peeta's cameo has now led to some controversy, but there's nevertheless no question that Lawrence and Hutcherson's role in the movie contributed to the still growing success of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.
